'''''Galinsoga quadriradiata''''' is a species of flowering plant in the family [[Asteraceae]] which is known by several common names, including '''shaggy soldier''',<ref>{{PLANTS|id=GAQU|taxon=Galinsoga quadriradiata|accessdate=19 January 2016}}</ref><ref name=BSBI07>{{BSBI 2007 |access-date=2014-10-17}}</ref> '''Peruvian daisy''', '''hairy galinsoga'''. Despite the common name, the plant's native home is apparently central [[Mexico]], although it has become an [[introduced species]] in many other places (North and South America, Europe, Japan, Philippines, the northern India, Nepal, etc.).<ref name=k>[http://www.efloras.org/florataxon.aspx?flora_id=1&taxon_id=200023970 Flora of North America, ''Galinsoga quadriradiata'' Ruiz & Pavón, 1798. ]</ref><ref name=c>[https://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/page/663378#page/359/mode/1up Canne-Hilliker, Judith Marie. 1977.  Rhodora 79(819): 353-364] in English, line drawing on page 354, around the world distribution map on page 359</ref> It is sometimes considered a weed.<ref name="Weeds of the South"></ref>

==Description==
Shaggy soldier is an annual [[herbaceous plant|herb]] about 25 cm (10 in.) tall (exceptionally up to 80 cm) and opposite leaves. It is so highly branched that it produces two side shoots at just about every node. The stems, leaves and bracts are all sparsely to densely hairy, with a mixture of glandular and simple hairs. The lower leaves are ovate and about 5 to 9 cm long and toothed, while the upper ones are smaller and more lanceolate. They all have petioles about 1 cm long and lack stipules.<ref name=Stace>{{Cite book |last=Stace |first=C.A. |title=New Flora of the British Isles |publisher=C & M Floristics |year=2019 |isbn=978-1-5272-2630-2 |edition=4th |location=Middlewood Green}}</ref><ref name=Sell4>{{cite book |last1=Sell |first1=Peter |last2=Murrell |first2=Gina |title=Flora of Great Britain and Ireland, vol. 4 |date=2006 |publisher=Cambridge University Press |location=Cambridge}}</ref>
[[File:Peruvian daisy.JPG|thumb|The leaves are ovate and toothed.]]

A typical plant will produce numerous flower heads, arranged in threes (technically, dichasial cymes) with 2 cm long [[Peduncle (botany)|peduncles]] at the tip of every branch. Each flower head is around 5 mm across and contains about 25 tiny (3 mm) yellow disc florets with five lobes at the ends, and five widely-spaced, larger (5 mm), petal-like, white ray florets with 2 or 3 crenate teeth. Both the disc and ray florets are fertile, but the disc florets are bisexual while the ray florets are female.<ref name="Sell4" />

The fruits are 1 to 1.5 mm long brown to black achenes, tapered at the base and [[Awn (botany)|awned]] with a white [[Pappus (botany)|pappus]].<ref name="Weeds of the South">{{cite book |last1=Bryson |first1=Charles T. |last2=DeFelice |first2=Michael S. |title=Weeds of the South |date=2009 |publisher=University of Georgia Press |location=Athens, Georgia |isbn=0-8203-3046-9 |pages=78}}</ref>

==Identification==
Shaggy soldier is usually a hairy plant, whereas the otherwise similar [[Galinsoga parviflora|gallant soldier]] tends to be more-or-less hairless, but these characters are insufficient for accurate identification. To be confident, it is important to check (with a hand lens) that shaggy soldier has simple (not forked) scales on the receptacle, and scales in the pappus with hairy margins and a long, thin point at the top.<ref name="Stace" />
[[File:Galinsoga quadriradiata 15-p.bot-galin.cilia-20.jpg|thumb|none|The pappus scales have fringed margins and an elongated, fine tip.]]

In the seedling phase, the plant has very short hypocotyls and smooth, club-shaped cotyledons with a slightly indented apex.<ref name="Weeds of the South"></ref>

==Uses==
[[File:Galinsoga quadriradiata macro.jpg|thumb|[[Macro photography|Macro photograph]] of a shaggy soldier flower showing ray and disk florets.]]
''Galinsoga quadriradiata'' and its cousin ''[[Galinsoga parviflora]]'' are both edible and can be used as a pot herb or in salads, although outside of their native range they have not been widely adopted as a culinary item other than in China. ''G. parviflora'' is preferred as a salad green due to its non-hairy leaves. If you happen to live in a tropical region, care must be taken to not confuse them with the distantly related, and visually similar, ''[[Tridax procumbens]]''.
